walkthroughs.body_html:
Unit 1: Writing for Purpose and Audience and Reading to Access Non-fiction and Media Texts — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Unit 1: Writing for Purpose and Audience and Reading to Access Non-fiction and Media Texts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Unit 1: Writing for Purpose and Audience and Reading to Access Non-fiction and Media Texts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: Skimming
Scanning
Reflecting
Inferring

mcqs.q: Why do text types have predictable features?
options: Skinner believed children couldn't learn language until age five.
Conventions develop because they serve communicative purpose — a recipe needs imperatives because it instructs; a news report needs the inverted pyramid because of how readers scan.
Text types have fixed features just because tradition says so.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.

mcqs.q: What is Skinner's behaviourist view of language acquisition?
options: Skinner believed in an innate grammar module.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.
Children learn language through imitation and operant conditioning — they are reinforced for correct utterances and corrected for errors.
Skinner believed children couldn't learn language until age five.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a phoneme and a grapheme?
options: A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound in a language; a grapheme is the written letter or letters that represent it.
Phonemes are letters and graphemes are syllables.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.
Phonemes are vowels and graphemes are consonants.
